USTR'S NEW TARIFF PROPOSALS. WHAT LIFESTYLE BRANDS NEED TO KNOW.

Your sourcing map just got redrawn, and the clock is already running.

Today the U.S. Trade Representative wrapped up its Section 301 investigations into "structural excess capacity" and found that the trade practices of 14 economies hurt U.S. commerce. 

It has now proposed new tariffs on all of them. 

None of this is final yet. 

But for anyone sourcing apparel, footwear or home goods overseas, this is the moment to start planning.

WHO GETS HIT HARDEST

Vietnam has the highest proposed rate, up to 35%, and textiles, apparel and footwear are named directly. India could see up to 25%, and China up to 20% on most goods. Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia are all looking at 18%, with Bangladesh's garment sector and Cambodia's and Indonesia's apparel industries called out by name. The EU, Japan, Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland sit at 15%.

THE FINE PRINT MATTERS

These rates are ceilings. They're calculated net of existing tariffs, and every country has a list of exempt products. Several rates are also up for negotiation. Vietnam could drop to 20%, India to 17% and Singapore to 10% if they reach trade agreements. Your actual exposure depends on HTS codes, so look at the product annexes, not the headline numbers.

WHERE THERE'S NOWHERE TO HIDE

The usual escape routes are all on this list. Shifting production from China to Vietnam or Bangladesh doesn't save you much when every major Asian sourcing country is facing a similar rate. That changes the math on nearshoring, on dual sourcing, and on how much pricing power you really have.

THE TIMELINE

Written comments and requests to testify are due January 5, 2027. Public hearings start January 25. That means Fall 2027 costing is happening while the rules are still being written.

WHAT I'D DO THIS WEEK

Pull your landed cost by country and by HTS code. Model your margins at the proposed rates and at the negotiated rates. Talk to your factories about splitting costs, and figure out which SKUs can carry a price increase and which ones can't. 

If one of these tariffs would really hurt your business, think about filing a comment. 

The brands that model this now will have choices. 

The ones that wait will just have to react.

Batam as Singapore’s Digital Spillover Hub: Engineering Tier-IV Power Reliability and Cross-Border Low-Latency Infrastructure

As Singapore enforces strict power, water, and carbon-efficiency thresholds on new data center allocations, Batam has emerged as Southeast Asia’s premier digital spillover hub—located just 20 kilometers across the Singapore Strait with sub-3-millisecond latency potential. Anchored by Special Economic Zones (KEKs) such as Nongsa Digital Park, Batam offers hyperscale and AI-ready campus developers rapid land scalability and direct proximity to Singapore’s financial and cloud ecosystem. 

Yet turning geographic proximity into institutional bankability requires far more than proximity alone. 

From an energy investment origination and enterprise risk governance perspective, Batam data center campuses reach institutional financial close only when Tier-IV redundant power architecture, cross-border subsea fiber diversity, and clean energy transition pathways are engineered upfront.

Developing hyperscale capacity on an islanded grid without dedicated dual-substation redundancy, diverse subsea cable landings, and verifiable low-carbon power exposes sponsors to SLA penalties and tenant hesitation.

Six core pillars define institutional origination for Tier-IV power reliability and cross-border infrastructure in Batam:

 1. Dual-Substation Redundancy & Island Grid Stability: Engineering independent 150 kV/20 kV feeds from PLN Batam—paired with grid-forming Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and N+1/2N backup generation—eliminates single-point-of-failure risks on an islanded power system.

 2. Cross-Border Subsea Fiber Diversity & Low-Latency Routing: Securing multiple physically diverse subsea fiber-optic cable landings connecting Batam directly to Singapore’s carrier-neutral data centers guarantees sub-3ms round-trip latency and route resilience.

 3. 24/7 Clean Power & Cross-Border Green Corridor Alignment: Integrating utility-scale solar-plus-BESS, regional renewable energy certificates (RECs), and emerging Indonesia–Singapore clean-power interconnection frameworks satisfies global hyperscaler decarbonization mandates.

The internet changed how businesses reach people. AI goes further: like electricity, it can power almost every part of how a business runs. That was ShopBack's view at Singapore FinTech Festival, where Matthew Chng, Senior Staff Software Engineer, joined speakers from Tencent Cloud, Nucleus Software andSalesforce on what it takes to move AI agents from pilot to production.

At ShopBack, that shift began in engineering. Every engineering team now hands work to agents through a software factory: a harness that breaks each task into small steps, checks every one and keeps a record, so output is verified rather than assumed. Human judgement scales with the stakes. Where a mistake is easy to undo, the team moves quickly and corrects as it goes. Where it touches the numbers or cannot be undone, a second engineer double-checks it.

The bigger shift is beyond engineering. As Matthew put it, the limit is no longer the technology but the processes built around how people used to work. When data that once took a week to gather takes a minute, a process designed around that week is worth rethinking. Not every process needs rebuilding: in others, AI simply improves what already works.

An AI-native company is not defined by how many agents it runs. It is defined by what it trusts them with, and the discipline behind that trust.

My first night in Jakarta, I sat alone in a small room and wondered if I had made a mistake.

I knew the system. I did not know anyone.

Just a year before, I was sitting in an office in Bengaluru, writing code for a banking system. Now I was far from home, setting up that system for a bank. 

I was scared of getting it wrong. But I stayed.

2005: Jakarta. My first go-live, far from home.
2006: Croatia. Four years of learning how a national bank really works.
2010: Malta, Denmark and Indonesia, one after another.
2015: Africa. Leading programmes in many countries.

Today: Leading banking programmes at VeriPark across the Middle East and Australia.

Somewhere in those years, the engineer who was scared of mistakes became the person his team looked at when things went wrong at 2 AM.

Those years taught me three things:

1. Say the hard thing early. Bad news told late always costs more.
2. Nobody gives you credibility. You earn it, go-live by go-live.
3. Your team watches your face before they read your email. Staying calm is a skill.

That scared engineer in Jakarta is still inside me. He is the reason I sit next to my team when things get hard.

If you are far from home or feeling not ready, keep going. It gets lighter.

Blanking, piercing, bending, forming, and drawing are NOT the same operation. ⚙️

They may happen on the same stamping line, but each serves a different purpose.

Understanding the difference helps engineers design better tooling, and helps buyers ask the right questions before approving a die.

Let's break it down. 👇

✂️ 1️⃣ Blanking
The punch cuts a shape out of sheet metal, and the removed piece is the intended product. The remaining sheet becomes scrap or skeleton material.

🕳️ 2️⃣ Piercing
The punch creates holes or openings in the material. Here, the hole is the feature you need, while the removed slug is scrap.

📐 3️⃣ Bending
The material is forced around a punch or die to create an angle or shape. The metal is reshaped without intentionally cutting through it.

🔧 4️⃣ Forming
A broader category of operations that change the shape of sheet metal. This can include flanging, embossing, curling, and other features that do not simply cut material away.

🥣 5️⃣ Drawing
In deep drawing, a punch pushes a sheet metal blank into a die cavity to create a three dimensional shape, such as a cup or housing. Material flows into the cavity, so blank holder force and material properties matter.

Why does this matter in real production?

Because every operation creates different tooling demands.

A piercing operation needs suitable cutting clearance. Bending requires control of springback. Deep drawing needs careful control of material flow to reduce wrinkling and tearing.

Mix these requirements up during die design, and you risk dimensional problems, defects, extra adjustments, and higher production costs.

The goal isn't just to make the metal take a new shape.

It's to achieve the required geometry, repeatability, and quality throughout production.

My first night in Jakarta, I sat alone in a small room and wondered if I had made a mistake.

I knew the system. I did not know anyone.

Just a year before, I was sitting in an office in Bengaluru, writing code for a banking system. Now I was far from home, setting up that system for a bank. 

I was scared of getting it wrong. But I stayed.

2005: Jakarta. My first go-live, far from home.
2006: Croatia. Four years of learning how a national bank really works.
2010: Malta, Denmark and Indonesia, one after another.
2015: Africa. Leading programmes in many countries.

Today: Leading banking programmes at VeriPark across the Middle East and Australia.

Somewhere in those years, the engineer who was scared of mistakes became the person his team looked at when things went wrong at 2 AM.

Those years taught me three things:

1. Say the hard thing early. Bad news told late always costs more.
2. Nobody gives you credibility. You earn it, go-live by go-live.
3. Your team watches your face before they read your email. Staying calm is a skill.

That scared engineer in Jakarta is still inside me. He is the reason I sit next to my team when things get hard.

If you are far from home or feeling not ready, keep going. It gets lighter.

Meet Graham.

Graham is a resilient expat. He is a corporate survivor. He is a global professional. He is enduring a difficult assignment in Southeast Asia.

At least, that is what his internal HR file says. Right next to his contract that includes a $50,000 hardship allowance.

Graham is from the UK. Graham works for a multinational engineering firm. Graham has lived in Jakarta for three years. Graham lives in a company-paid apartment in SCBD with a private pool. Graham has a full-time housekeeper named Sari. Graham has a personal driver named Pak Yanto.

But Graham is suffering.

Graham tells his headquarters in London that Jakarta is a highly challenging environment. He says the pollution is toxic. He says the traffic is unbearable. He says the local government is unstable. He says his mental health is suffering.

Because Graham says these things, the company pays him extra. They pay him a hardship bonus. They pay for his international school fees. They pay for his business-class flights home. They even equalize his taxes so he does not have to pay Indonesian income tax.

On weekends, Graham uses his hardship bonus to rent a luxury villa in Bali. He posts photos on Instagram. So grateful for this beautiful life.

The local engineer who works in the exact same office as Graham is named Rina. Rina breathes the same pollution. Rina sits in the same traffic. Rina deals with the same government. But Rina does not get a hardship allowance. Rina earns $15,000 a year. And because it is her home country, she does not have the option to leave.

Graham calls it compensation for a difficult assignment. Rina calls it a Tuesday.

This satire is not an attack on global mobility, corporate compensation, or the challenges of living abroad. This is an audit of the vocabulary. It is about the Hardship Allowance Hypocrite™ ecosystem. It is a system where Western professionals perform suffering to extract more wealth from their corporations. It is about the man who calls a city of 10 million people a war zone so he can afford a villa in Bali. If you are calling a city a hardship posting while your driver is stuck in traffic outside your luxury apartment, you are not surviving. You are exploiting.

Graham is not a survivor. Graham is a hardship allowance hypocrite™. And today we audit the danger pay and the Bali villa.

Great to be in Jakarta this week for the 10th Waste Management & Waste to Energy Asia Summit 2026 – Indonesia Focus, organised by INBC Global at Hotel Bidakara (25–27 November).
 
We were glad to present MARTIN Technologies at the summit and share how our proven waste-to-energy technology can help Indonesia and the wider ASEAN region turn municipal solid waste into reliable, clean energy.
 
Indonesia's push on waste-to-energy is gaining real momentum, and the conversations here, with developers, EPC contractors, utilities and policymakers, showed how much appetite there is for technology that is bankable, reliable and built for the region's waste.
 
Our thanks to INBC Global for a well-run event, to the partners and fellow exhibitors, and to everyone who stopped by to talk with us. We look forward to continuing these discussions and to building partnerships across Indonesia and Southeast Asia.

A great week in Singapore! Thank you to OCBC for inviting me to participate in an insightful SAF roundtable discussion on “Building Bankable SAF Corridors for SAF” , followed by my two days at the SAF APAC Congress.

From India’s anticipated SAF policy announcement, Indonesia’s ambitious biofuels programme to Singapore’s centralised SAF procurement approach, we are seeing progress across the region.  At the same time, Malaysia has deferred its 1% SAF mandate from 2027 to 2030 and South Korea’s longer-term blending targets remain subject to review.  The direction remains clear although the pace and approaches differ. My key takeaways: 

✅ Policy certainty, revenue certainty, feedstock security, creditworthiness of sponsors / developers to technology readiness are all important in translating project ambitions into investment decisions.

✅ Demand aggregation will be critical. While airlines are committed to decarbonisation, aggregated demand and mechanisms such as Book & Claim could play an important role in accelerating offtake.

✅ SAF extends beyond commercial aviation. It was interesting to hear perspectives from both commercial and defence aviation, where drivers for adopting sustainable fuels may differ — from achieving net-zero ambitions to strengthening energy security and supply resilience.

Next stop — Jakarta, where I will moderating a panel tomorrow at the  Biogas Biomass Biofuels & SAF Asia Summit 2026 with my topic “Building a Sustainable Feedstock Ecosystem: Unlocking Indonesia’s UCO, Biomass & Waste-to-Biofuel Potential.” Looking forward to hearing insights from my fellow panellists and continuing the conversation on one of the most fundamental building blocks of a sustainable biofuels industry — Feedstock! . 
At FGE NexantECA, we have and are supporting projects globally across the development lifecycle — from early-stage feasibility and investment assessment through to financial close and construction monitoring.  If you would like to learn more about the evolving SAF / renewable fuels industry landscape or how we can support your project, please feel free to reach out.  Happy Thursday everyone.
